droplets.description: Write JavaScript that waits for network requests and timers without freezing the page.
droplets.overview: Network requests and timers take time, and JavaScript doesn't stop to wait for them. This droplet explains the event loop in plain terms, then shows how promises and async/await keep asynchronous code readable and correct.
droplets.funFact: Promises became part of the JavaScript language in ECMAScript 2015, and the async and await keywords followed two years later in ECMAScript 2017.
learningObjectives: Explain how the event loop runs callbacks after slow work finishes
Chain promises with then and catch, and combine them with Promise.all

content.text: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, which means it does one thing at a time. A network request can take hundreds of milliseconds. If JavaScript stopped and waited for it, nothing else could happen in the meantime: clicks wouldn't respond and the page couldn't update.

So JavaScript doesn't wait. It hands slow work like timers and network requests to the browser, or to Node.js on a server, and moves on to the next line. When the work finishes, a function you provided, called a callback, is queued to run.
A callback is a function you pass to other code so it can call it later, for example when a timer fires or a request finishes.
The event loop in plain terms
JavaScript runs the current piece of code from start to finish without interruption.
Meanwhile, the browser handles timers and network requests in the background.
When one of them finishes, its callback joins a queue.
Whenever JavaScript has nothing left to run, the event loop takes the next callback from the queue and runs it.

droplets.name: Big-O Notation Without the Fear
droplets.description: Read Big-O and spot it in code, so you can tell when a program will slow down as its data grows.
droplets.overview: Big-O describes how the work an algorithm does grows as its input grows. This droplet explains what it measures, walks through the common classes from O(1) to O(n²), and shows how to spot them in Python code.
droplets.funFact: The mathematician Paul Bachmann introduced Big-O notation in an 1894 book on number theory, decades before the first electronic computers.
learningObjectives: Explain what Big-O measures and why it drops constants
Compare the common classes from O(1) to O(n²)
Estimate the Big-O of loops, nested loops, halving and membership checks in Python

content.text: You can time your code with a stopwatch, but the number you get depends on your laptop, what else is running, and the input you happened to try. Big-O answers a more useful question:
as the input grows, how fast does the work grow?

Say your club website keeps its member list in a Python list, and checking whether someone is a member means looking at each name in turn. With 100 members, that's up to 100 comparisons. With 10,000 members, it's up to 10,000. The work grows in step with the size of the input, and Big-O writes that as O(n), where n is the size of the input.
Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time, or the memory it uses, grows as the size of its input, called n, grows.
Here's that membership check in code:

If the name is first in the list, the function returns after one comparison. If the name isn't there at all, it compares against every member. Unless someone says otherwise, a Big-O describes the worst case, since that's a guarantee: no input of that size makes the code do more work. So
Big-O doesn't count seconds. It counts basic steps, like comparisons, additions and lookups, as a function of n, and it cares about how that count grows more than about its exact value.
Suppose an algorithm takes 3n² + 5n + 2 steps. For small inputs every term matters, but as n grows, the n² term takes over:
At n = 1,000, the 5n + 2 part is less than 1 percent of the total. So Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing term and drops its constant factor:

Constants like the 3 depend on details such as what you count as one step, and the seconds each step takes depend on your machine. Neither changes the shape of the growth: double n, and the work still roughly quadruples. That shape is what Big-O captures.

Formally, Big-O is an upper bound, so an O(n) algorithm is technically O(n²) too. In practice, people quote the tightest class that fits, and algorithms courses add Big-Omega and Big-Theta for lower and tight bounds.

props.question: An algorithm takes 4n + 10 steps on an input of size n. After dropping constants and smaller terms, what is its Big-O?

content.text: Most code you'll write lands in one of a handful of Big-O classes. Here they are from slowest-growing to fastest-growing:
Looking up a student by ID in a Python dictionary
The work stays about the same
Finding a word in a printed dictionary by opening it in the middle, then halving
Reading every name on a sign-up sheet
Sorting a class roster with sorted()
Every club member shaking hands with every other member
A few notes on the table:
Dictionary and set lookups are O(1) on average. In rare cases they can be slower, but you can usually treat them as constant.
The logs here are base 2, so log n is roughly how many times you can halve n before you reach 1. The base doesn't matter in Big-O, because switching bases only multiplies by a constant.
The handshake example is quadratic because n members make n(n - 1)/2 handshakes, and that grows like n².
The gap between classes is small for small inputs and enormous for large ones:
Suppose each step takes one microsecond. On a million items, n log n steps take about 20 seconds, while n² steps take more than 11 days.

Some algorithms grow faster still. Exponential time, O(2ⁿ), doubles the work every time n grows by just one. That's what happens when code tries every possible subset, like every team you could form from a class of students.
Big-O tells you how code scales, not how fast it is on small inputs. For a list of 20 items, an O(n²) algorithm can beat an O(n log n) one that has more overhead.

props.question: If an O(n²) function takes 1 second on 1,000 students, you would expect it to take about 4 seconds on 2,000 students.

For each email, the inner loop checks every email after it. In the worst case that's (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1 comparisons, which adds up to n(n - 1)/2, so the function is O(n²). When nested loops run over two different inputs, say n students and m courses, the total is O(n × m).

This is binary search on a sorted list of student IDs. Each pass through the loop throws away half of what's left, so a million IDs take at most 20 passes. Code that halves its input on every step is O(log n). Python's

Building the set takes O(m) once and the loop takes O(n), so the function is now O(n + m). Watch for other lines that hide a loop, too:
A single line can hide a loop. Calling in, index or remove on a list inside a loop over a list of similar size turns an O(n) loop into O(n²).

droplets.name: Landing Your First Co-op
droplets.description: Get your materials ready, apply with focus, handle interviews and start your first co-op well.
droplets.overview: Your first co-op search can feel like an extra course. This droplet walks you through getting ready, applying and interviewing, and choosing an offer, with advice that works for whatever kind of role you're aiming for.
droplets.funFact: The first co-op program began in 1906 at the University of Cincinnati, where engineering dean Herman Schneider had students alternate between classes and paid jobs with local employers.
learningObjectives: Prepare a tailored resume and a portfolio of your projects
Track and tailor each application
Answer behavioral questions with the STAR method
Compare offers and make a strong start

content.text: A co-op search goes more smoothly when your materials are ready before you start applying. Three things matter most: a good relationship with your co-op advisor, a resume aimed at the roles you want, and a place where employers can see your work.
Your co-op advisor knows how the process works in your program and has helped other students through it. Meet them before you start applying, and come prepared:
Bring a draft of your resume.
Bring a short list of roles or industries you're curious about, even if you're not sure yet.
Ask how the process and timeline work for your program.
Ask what has helped past students with goals like yours.
Keep your co-op advisor updated as things happen, from interviews to offers to problems. They can only help with what they know about.
You probably have a general resume already. For co-op, the key step is tailoring it:
Keep a master resume with every project, job and activity you've done.
For each kind of role, make a version that leads with your most relevant work. A data analyst version might open with your SQL project, and a software version with the app your team built.
Use the posting's words where they're true. If it asks for REST API experience and you built one, say "REST API" rather than something vaguer like "backend work".
Only list skills you can answer questions about. Anything on your resume is fair game in an interview.
Before your first co-op, your projects are your experience. Make them easy to find:
Pin your best repositories to your GitHub profile.
Give each one a README that says what it does, how to run it, and which parts you built, especially for group projects.
Clean up before you share: remove passwords and API keys, and make sure the code runs.
If your work is visual, like a club website, a simple portfolio page with screenshots and links works well.

options.text: Send the same resume to every posting
Keep a master resume and make a tailored version for each kind of role
List every tool you've ever heard of
Leave off your projects to keep it short

props.question: You're applying to both data analyst and software roles. What should you do with your resume?

content.text: Once you start applying, the work is keeping track, tailoring each application, and getting ready to talk about yourself.
A simple spreadsheet keeps you from losing track of where each application stands:
Follow up if no reply by Friday
Talk to your co-op advisor before the deadline
Add columns for the date you applied, deadlines and contacts if they help. Update the sheet every time something changes.

Read each posting closely before you apply. Pick the two or three requirements that matter most, and make sure your resume shows evidence of each one near the top. If you write a cover letter, connect one specific project to what the team does. Tailoring takes time, so spend it on roles you actually want.
Interviews often include behavioral questions, like "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate." The interviewer wants one specific story, not a general claim like "I'm a team player."
The STAR method structures a story in four parts: Situation, Task, Action and Result.
Here's a STAR answer about a group project:
In my CS 3200 group project, one teammate stopped replying two weeks before the deadline.
Our reporting page depended on their queries, so we needed a plan to finish on time.
I messaged them directly and learned they had three exams that week. We moved two of their queries to me, and I set up a 15-minute check-in twice a week.
We submitted on time, earned an A, and kept the check-ins for the rest of the semester.
A few habits make STAR answers stronger:
Spend most of your answer on the Action, and say "I" for the things you did.
Prepare four or five stories from projects, jobs, clubs and classes. You can adapt each one to several questions.
Practice out loud, and aim for about two minutes per answer.
Have two or three questions ready to ask the interviewer at the end.

lessons.name: Choosing an offer and starting well

content.text: An offer is good news, and it's also a decision. Take the time to choose well, then set yourself up for a strong first few weeks.
Pay matters, but it isn't the only thing to compare:
What will you build or analyze, and what will you learn?
Who will your manager be, and will you have a mentor or other co-ops nearby?
Location, commute, hours, and whether the role is in person, hybrid or remote.
How does the role set you up for your next co-op or your first job?
Questions to ask before you accept
It's normal to ask an employer questions before you decide. Good ones include:
"What would a typical week look like for me?"
"What did your last co-op work on?"
"Who would I work with day to day, and how does the team give feedback?"
"Which tools and languages does the team use?"
Talk to your co-op advisor before you accept or turn down an offer. They can explain how offers and deadlines work in your program.
Treat accepting an offer as a firm commitment. Backing out later lets down a team that planned around you, so accept only when you're ready to commit.
The first few weeks set the tone for the rest of your co-op:
Try a problem on your own first, then ask for help and explain what you've tried.
Write things down: setup steps, names, acronyms and answers, so you don't have to ask twice.
Ask your manager what a successful co-op looks like to them, and set up a regular check-in.
Ask for feedback a few weeks in, not just at the end.
Keep a weekly log of what you worked on and learned. It makes your next resume and interviews much easier to prepare.

props.question: Besides pay, name two things to compare when you're choosing between co-op offers.
props.correctAnswer: For example, the work you'd do and what you'd learn, your manager and mentorship, the location and schedule, and how the role fits your goals.

droplets.name: How Hash Tables Work
droplets.description: Why a Python dict can find any key quickly, even with millions of entries.
droplets.overview: A hash table turns each key into an array index, so finding a value doesn't mean searching through everything. This droplet covers hash functions, collisions and resizing, and how Python's dict and set put them to work.
droplets.funFact: Since Python 3.7, dictionaries are guaranteed to keep keys in the order you inserted them, a behavior that began as a side effect of a more compact dict design in Python 3.6.
learningObjectives: Explain how a hash function maps a key to a bucket
Compare chaining and open addressing for handling collisions
Describe how load factor and resizing keep lookups fast
Choose valid dictionary keys and predict when lookups slow down

content.text: Say your club website keeps its 5,000 members in a Python list. To check whether "Jordan Lee" is a member, Python compares names one at a time until it finds a match or reaches the end. Double the members and the worst case doubles too.
A hash table skips that search. It stores entries in an array of slots called
, and it computes which bucket a key belongs in instead of looking for it. Arrays are good at jumping straight to a position by its index, and a hash table puts that to work.
A hash function turns a key, like a student's name, into an integer called a hash. The hash table uses that integer to choose a bucket.

Finding a key's bucket takes two steps: hash the key, then take the remainder after dividing by the number of buckets. In Python, that remainder is always between 0 and one less than the number of buckets, so it's always a valid index.

props.code:
def simple_hash(key: str) -> int:
    total = 0
    for ch in key:
        total = total * 31 + ord(ch)
    return total

num_buckets = 8
print(simple_hash("Maya"))                  # 2390972
print(simple_hash("Maya") % num_buckets)    # 4
print(simple_hash("Jordan") % num_buckets)  # 4

content.text: returns a character's Unicode code point, so the function builds one large number from the letters of the name. To store Maya's record, the table puts it in bucket 4. To find it later, the table runs the same two steps, lands on bucket 4 again, and checks only what's there.
What makes a good hash function
While the table exists, the same key must always produce the same hash, or the table would look in the wrong bucket.
Keys should scatter across the buckets so that no bucket gets crowded.
Every insert and every lookup starts by hashing the key.

Here's what goes wrong with a weak one. If you only added up the character codes, "Mary" and "Myra" would both hash to 409, because they use the same letters, and so would every other arrangement of those letters. Multiplying by 31 at each step makes the order of the letters matter, so
Even a good hash function can send two keys to the same bucket. Notice that "Jordan" also landed in bucket 4. That's a
, and every hash table needs a plan for it.

options.text: Different keys always get different hashes
A key gets the same hash every time the table hashes it
Every hash is smaller than the number of buckets
Keys come back out in sorted order

content.text: There are far more possible keys than buckets, so collisions can't be avoided, and by chance they start long before the table is full. Hash tables handle them in one of two main ways.

, each bucket holds a small list of key and value pairs. Inserting adds a pair to the bucket's list, or replaces the value if the key is already there. Looking up a key means going to its bucket and comparing keys until one matches.
function. A lookup only compares the keys in one bucket, and that list stays short as long as keys are spread out.

, every entry lives directly in the array, one per slot. When a key's slot is taken, the table probes other slots in a fixed order. The simplest order, linear probing, tries the next slot, then the next, wrapping around at the end. A lookup follows the same path until it finds the key or reaches an empty slot. Here's linear probing with

content.text: With open addressing, deleting can't just empty a slot. If Maya's bucket were cleared, a search for Jordan would stop at the empty bucket 4 and wrongly report him missing, so implementations leave a marker in the slot instead.
Java's HashMap uses chaining. The standard Python interpreter uses open addressing for dict, with a probe order that jumps around the table instead of stepping one slot at a time.

As the load factor rises, chains and probe paths get longer, so lookups slow down. To prevent that, a hash table resizes once its load factor passes a limit: it allocates a bigger array, usually about twice the size, and reinserts every entry. Java's HashMap, for example, does this when its load factor passes 0.75 by default.
Every entry has to be rehashed, because its bucket depends on the number of buckets. With
and 16 buckets instead of 8, Maya moves from bucket 4 to bucket 12 while Jordan stays in bucket 4, so their collision goes away.
A resize copies every entry, so the insert that triggers it is slow. Because the table doubles each time, though, resizes get rarer as it grows, and the average cost per insert stays constant.

content.text: If you check membership inside a loop, such as finding which of 2,000 applicants are already club members, turn the member list into a set first. Each check then takes one hash instead of a scan through the whole list.
A key's hash can't change while it's in the table. If it did, the table would look for the key in the wrong bucket. That's why Python only accepts
objects as dict keys and set items.
Objects of your own classes are hashable by default, but each one is only equal to itself. If you define
so that two objects with the same data are equal, Python makes the class unhashable unless you also define
. A frozen dataclass defines both for you:
Objects that are equal must have equal hashes. Otherwise a dict can't find a key when you look it up with an equal copy.

On average, lookups, inserts and deletes take constant time, written O(1), as long as the hash function spreads keys well and the load factor stays bounded. In the worst case, every key lands in the same bucket, the table behaves like a list, and each operation takes O(n) time.

That worst case can happen by accident, with a poor hash function, or on purpose: an attacker who can predict your hashes can send a web server thousands of keys that all collide. To make that hard, Python mixes a random value into string hashes each time it starts, so
gives a different number in each run. Compare hashes within one run of a program, and never save them to a file or database.

droplets.description: Hash passwords so a stolen database doesn't hand attackers your users' accounts.
droplets.overview: Any database can leak, so passwords have to be stored in a form that's close to useless to an attacker. This droplet explains why plain hashes fail, how salts and slow password hashes like Argon2 fix that, and how to use them correctly in Python.

lessons.name: Why plain text and plain hashes fail

content.text: Plan as if your database will leak someday. It can happen through SQL injection, a misconfigured backup, a stolen laptop or an access key pushed to a public repository. What matters is what an attacker can do with the password column once they have it.

If you store passwords exactly as people typed them, a breach hands over every one of them. The damage doesn't stop at your site. Many people reuse passwords, so attackers try each leaked email and password on other services, which is called credential stuffing. A leak from a club website can unlock someone's email account.

Encrypting the passwords doesn't fix this. Anything encrypted can be decrypted with the key, and the key usually lives on the same servers the attacker just got into. Your server never needs to read a password back. It only needs to check whether a login attempt matches, and that's a job for a one-way function.
A cryptographic hash function turns any input into a fixed-size output, and it's designed so that you can't work backward from the output to the input.
Storing a SHA-256 hash of each password looks like it solves the problem:
The same password always gives the same hash.

Everyone who chose "password" has the same entry in your table, so cracking one cracks them all. Attackers also precompute hashes for millions of common and leaked passwords, then look up stolen hashes in those tables almost instantly.

SHA-256 is designed to be quick, which is great for checking a download and terrible here. A single modern graphics card can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so an attacker can test huge lists of likely passwords against every stolen hash. MD5 and SHA-1, which you'll still find in old systems, are even faster.
A fast, general purpose hash like SHA-256 isn't safe for passwords, even with a salt. Use a hash designed for passwords.

Its output is too long to store in a database

content.text: is a random value generated for each user when they set a password. The system hashes the salt together with the password and stores the salt right next to the hash. The salt isn't a secret. Its job is to make every hash unique:
Two users with the same password get different hashes, so cracking one doesn't reveal the other.
Precomputed tables stop working, because an attacker would need a separate table for every salt.
An attacker has to guess against each hash separately.
Generate a new salt from a secure random source every time a password is set or changed. Password hashing libraries do this for you. argon2-cffi, for example, uses 16 random bytes for each hash.

A salt doesn't make a single guess any slower. An attacker going after one account can still try billions of SHA-256 guesses per second. Password hashing functions are built to be slow instead, and you choose how slow with settings called the
A cost, where each step up doubles the work
Only uses the first 72 bytes of a password
A CPU and memory cost, block size and parallelism
Needs lots of memory, which makes custom cracking hardware expensive

Curly braces insert a JavaScript value into the markup, as in

Props are how a parent component passes data to a child, like arguments to a function. You write them like HTML attributes:
String values go in quotes. Anything else, like a number, an array or a function, goes in curly braces. React gathers the props into one object and passes it to the component, and

A prop is a value a parent component passes to a child. The child reads it like a function argument and never changes it.
A component must never change its own props. If a

To show a component for each item in an array, use

droplets.description: Write functions that call themselves, trace them on the call stack, and know when a loop is the better tool.
droplets.overview: A recursive function solves a problem by solving a smaller version of the same problem. This droplet covers base cases and recursive cases, what the call stack does while recursion runs, and why recursion suits nested data like folder trees.
droplets.funFact: The name of the GNU free software project is a recursive acronym that stands for GNU's Not Unix.
learningObjectives: Write a recursive function with a base case and a recursive case
Trace recursive calls on the call stack and explain a RecursionError
Use recursion to process nested data, and recognize when a loop is simpler

content.text: is a function that calls itself. That sounds circular, but it works as long as each call hands a smaller version of the problem to the next one, until the problem is small enough to answer directly.
Take adding up the credits on your schedule. The total of
. That's the same problem, one item shorter. Keep going and you reach the empty list, whose total is 0.

props.code:
def total_credits(credits):
    if not credits:  # base case: an empty list
        return 0
    return credits[0] + total_credits(credits[1:])  # recursive case


print(total_credits([4, 4, 1, 4]))  # 13

content.text: The base case is an input the function answers directly, without calling itself. The recursive case covers every other input by calling the function again on a smaller one.
that returns an answer without recursing. Here it's the empty list, whose total is 0.
that makes the problem smaller, calls the function on the smaller problem, and uses the result. Here
is the list without its first item, and the function adds
to the total of the rest.
The recursive case has to move toward the base case. If
passed along the same list instead of
, it would never reach the empty list, and the calls would continue until Python stopped them. The next lesson shows what that looks like.
When you write a recursive function, answer these in order:
What's the smallest input, and what's the answer for it?
How can I make the input smaller?
If the function already worked on the smaller input, how would I use that answer?

The third question takes practice. While you're writing the function, don't try to trace every call in your head. Assume the recursive call returns the right answer for the smaller input, and work out only the one step that's left.

Here's that process for reversing a string. The smallest inputs are strings of zero or one characters, which are their own reverse. A string gets smaller when you drop its first character. And once the rest of the string is reversed, the first character goes on the end.

content.text: When one function calls another, Python pauses the caller, runs the function it called, and picks up where it left off once that function returns. To keep track, it uses the

The call stack holds the function calls that have started but not yet returned. Each call has its own frame, with its own arguments and local variables.

    returns 5
returns 9

The call on the empty list is the last to start and the first to return. Then each waiting frame finishes its own addition with the value it got back: 4 + 0, then 1 + 4, then 4 + 5.
Each frame also has its own
. While the deepest call sees an empty list, the first call's

content.text: Adding up a flat list doesn't really need recursion, since a loop or

To count every file, count the files in this folder, then add the count for each subfolder. Counting a subfolder is the same problem on a smaller folder.

A plain loop struggles here, because you don't know ahead of time how deep the folders go. Recursion follows each branch as far down as it goes, then comes back up.

For a list of credits or a roster, a loop or a built-in like
Every level of recursion adds a frame, so the

Reach for recursion when a problem breaks into smaller problems of the same shape, like folders inside folders. For a flat list, a loop is simpler and can't hit the recursion limit.

droplets.name: Designing REST APIs
droplets.description: Name your resources, pick the right methods and status codes, and return JSON that clients can rely on.
droplets.overview: A REST API lets other programs read and change your app's data over HTTP. This droplet covers how to name resources, which methods and status codes to use, and how to shape requests and responses so clients can depend on them.
droplets.funFact: The term REST, short for representational state transfer, comes from Roy Fielding's 2000 doctoral dissertation at the University of California, Irvine.
learningObjectives: Name resources with clear, predictable URLs
Choose the right method and status code for each request
Design consistent JSON bodies, errors and pagination
Version an API without breaking its clients

content.text: A REST API organizes your app's data as
: the things it stores, like students, courses and enrollments. Each resource has its own URL, and clients use HTTP methods to read or change it.
Good URLs are predictable. Someone who has seen
should be able to guess the URL for course 7 without opening your docs.
A resource is a piece of data your API exposes at its own URL, such as one student or the list of all courses.
The URL names the thing. The HTTP method, covered in the next lesson, says what to do with it. That's why the URL doesn't need verbs like get or create.
Use a plural noun for a collection, and add an ID to get one item from it:

props.code:
GET /students       every student
GET /students/42    the student with ID 42
GET /courses        every course
GET /courses/7      the course with ID 7

content.text: Use lowercase letters, and separate words with hyphens, as in
When one resource belongs to another, nest it under its parent.
reads as "the enrollments of student 42", and
Keep nesting shallow. A path like
ties clients to one route through your data, when they could go straight to
. One level of nesting is usually enough.
The path identifies a resource. The query string, after the
, filters, sorts or searches a collection:

props.code:
GET /courses?credits=4
GET /students?search=patel
GET /students?sort=gpa&order=desc

content.text: Avoid making a new path for every filter, like
. Query parameters combine freely, so one collection URL covers every filter.

content.text: Every request pairs a method with a URL. The method says what the client wants to do, and the status code in the response says what happened.
Reads a resource without changing it
Creates a new resource in a collection
Replaces a resource with the one you send
Changes only the fields you send
PUT and PATCH are easy to mix up. PUT replaces the whole student, so you send every field. PATCH updates part of it, so you send only what changed:

props.code:
curl -i -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/students/42 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"major": "Data Science"}'

content.text: shows the status line and headers along with the response body.
Methods also make promises. GET is
: it shouldn't change any data, so clients and caches can repeat it freely. PUT and DELETE are
: sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once. POST is neither, so two identical POSTs can create two enrollments.

The first digit of a status code gives its category: 2xx means success, 3xx means a redirect, 4xx means the client sent something wrong, and 5xx means the server failed. These are the codes you'll use most:
The request worked and the response has a body
A POST created a new resource
The request worked and there's nothing to send back, often after a DELETE
The body is malformed or a field is invalid
The client isn't logged in, or its token is missing or expired
The client is logged in but isn't allowed to do this
The request clashes with current data, like enrolling a student twice
401 means the server doesn't know who you are. 403 means it knows who you are, and the answer is still no.
When a POST creates something, send 201 and a
header that points to the new resource:

props.code:
curl -i http://localhost:8000/students/42/enrollments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"course_id": 7, "semester": "Spring 2027"}'

content.text: this time, because sending a body with
makes curl use POST. Here's the response, trimmed to the lines that matter:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /students/42/enrollments/318
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 318, "student_id": 42, "course_id": 7, "semester": "Spring 2027", "grade": null}

Send and return JSON with a

droplets.name: Summarizing Data with GROUP BY
droplets.description: Turn rows into counts, totals and averages for each group with GROUP BY and HAVING.
droplets.overview: Aggregate functions turn many rows into one number, and GROUP BY gives you one of those numbers for each group. This droplet covers the five core aggregates, how they treat NULL, the grouping rule, and filtering groups with HAVING.
droplets.funFact: In PostgreSQL, writing GROUP BY ROLLUP (major) instead of GROUP BY major adds a grand total row to the results of the same query.
learningObjectives: Summarize a table with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
Predict how aggregate functions treat NULL values
Group rows with GROUP BY and follow the grouping rule
Filter groups with HAVING and rows with WHERE

content.text: An aggregate function combines many rows into one value. These five cover most of what you'll need:
The examples in this droplet use the

       MIN(gpa) AS lowest_gpa,
       MAX(gpa) AS highest_gpa,
       SUM(credits) AS total_credits
FROM students;

This returns 7 and 6, because Diego's GPA is NULL.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS enrollments,
       COUNT(grade) AS graded,

content.text: In the sample data, that's 41 enrollments from 7 students, and 26 of them are graded.
counts each student once, however many courses they take.
SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL, not 0, when there are no rows to aggregate. Write COALESCE(SUM(credits), 0) when you need a zero.

props.question: COUNT(grade) counts every row in enrollments, including rows where grade is NULL.

content.text: One number for the whole table is a start, but usually you want one per major, per course or per semester.
splits the rows into groups that share a value, then runs each aggregate once per group.

props.code:
SELECT major,
       COUNT(*) AS num_students,
       ROUND(AVG(gpa), 2) AS avg_gpa
FROM students
GROUP BY major
ORDER BY num_students DESC;

content.text: Each output row is one group. The Computer Science group holds four rows, for Maya, Priya, Diego and Noah, so its count is 4. Its average covers only the three of them with a GPA.
Every column in the SELECT list has to be either listed in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate function. Here's what happens when you break the rule:

props.code: ERROR:  column "students.name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function

content.text: The Computer Science group has four names, and PostgreSQL won't guess which one you want. You can fix it in two ways:
lists every name in the group, and
Add the column to GROUP BY. That changes the groups, though: grouping by major and name gives one group per student.
Every column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function.
GROUP BY works the same way on joined tables. This query counts the students in each course:

props.code:
SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled
FROM courses c
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.title
ORDER BY enrolled DESC;

content.text: The LEFT JOIN keeps courses that have no enrollments.
keeps two courses with the same title apart.

counts the row and reports 1. In the sample data, nobody has taken Cryptography yet, so it correctly shows 0.
With a LEFT JOIN, count a column from the right-hand table. Counting rows reports 1 for a course that has no enrollments.

props.question: Why does PostgreSQL reject SELECT major, name, COUNT(gpa) FROM students GROUP BY major?
props.correctAnswer: Each major's group contains several names, so there's no single name to show. The name column has to be listed in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate function.

content.text: filters groups after the aggregates are computed, so it's where conditions on aggregates go. This query keeps only the majors whose average GPA is above 3.5:

props.code:
SELECT major, ROUND(AVG(gpa), 2) AS avg_gpa
FROM students
GROUP BY major
HAVING AVG(gpa) > 3.5
ORDER BY avg_gpa DESC;

content.text: Data Science, at 3.40, is filtered out. You couldn't write this condition in WHERE, because WHERE looks at one row at a time, before any averages exist. PostgreSQL stops you with
aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE
Many queries need both. This one counts the students in each major who have at least 32 credits, then keeps the majors with at least two of them:

props.code:
SELECT major, COUNT(*) AS num_students
FROM students
WHERE credits >= 32
GROUP BY major
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

content.text: WHERE runs first and removes Diego, the only student with fewer than 32 credits. GROUP BY then forms three groups: Computer Science with 3 students, Data Science with 2 and Cybersecurity with 1. Last, HAVING drops Cybersecurity. The result has two rows, Computer Science with 3 and Data Science with 2. Without the WHERE clause, Computer Science would count 4.
SQL behaves as if it runs the clauses of a query in this order:
FROM and JOIN collect the rows.
This order explains two rules that trip people up. Aggregates can't go in WHERE, because the groups don't exist yet at that step. And in PostgreSQL, a SELECT alias like
works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE or HAVING, since the alias isn't defined until SELECT runs. That's why the average GPA query above repeats
in its HAVING clause instead of using
Put conditions on individual rows in WHERE and conditions on aggregates in HAVING.

droplets.name: SQL Window Functions
droplets.description: Rank, compare and total rows without collapsing them, using OVER and PARTITION BY.
droplets.overview: Window functions calculate across related rows while keeping every row in the result. This droplet covers PARTITION BY, the three ranking functions, running totals, and comparing rows with their neighbors using LAG and LEAD.
droplets.funFact: PostgreSQL added window functions in version 8.4, released in 2009, the same release that introduced WITH queries.
learningObjectives: Explain how a window function differs from GROUP BY
Rank rows within groups using ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
Compute running totals with an ordered window
Compare each row with its neighbors using LAG and LEAD

content.text: GROUP BY collapses each group into one row. That's right for a summary, but it throws away the individual rows. A
also calculates across a set of rows, but it keeps every row and adds its result as a new column.
table from the CS 3200 database, with seven students. Diego is in his first semester and doesn't have a GPA yet. Compare these two queries:
That returns three rows, one per major. Here's the window version:

props.code:
SELECT name, major, gpa,
       ROUND(AVG(gpa) OVER (PARTITION BY major), 2) AS major_avg
FROM students
ORDER BY major, name;

content.text: All seven students are still there, and each row carries its major's average. Diego has no GPA, but his row still gets the Computer Science average of 3.70.
A window is the set of rows a window function looks at when it computes the value for the current row.
is what makes a function a window function. Familiar aggregates like
splits the rows into partitions, one per major, and the function runs separately in each. Partitions are like groups, except the rows don't collapse.
Empty parentheses make the window the whole result.
puts the total number of rows on every row.
Because the result sits next to the row's own values, you can do math with it.
shows how far each student is above or below their major's average: Maya is 0.10 above, and Priya is 0.20 below.
Window functions are computed after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, when SELECT builds the output. That means you can't filter on one in WHERE. PostgreSQL rejects it:

props.code: ERROR:  window functions are not allowed in WHERE

content.text: To filter on a window result, compute it in a subquery or a WITH query first, then filter in the outer query. The next lesson does exactly that.

options.text: None, because it's an error to select name without grouping by it

props.question: The students table has 7 rows. How many rows does SELECT name, AVG(gpa) OVER (PARTITION BY major) FROM students return?

content.text: Put ORDER BY inside OVER and you can number the rows in that order. Three functions do this, and they differ only in how they handle ties:

props.code:
SELECT name, gpa,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY gpa DESC, name) AS row_number,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY gpa DESC) AS rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY gpa DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM students
WHERE gpa IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY gpa DESC, name;

content.text: gives every row a different number, even when values tie. Which tied row comes first is arbitrary unless you add a tiebreaker, which is why this query also orders by
gives tied rows the same rank, then skips ahead. Maya and Noah share 2nd place, so Ava is 4th.
gives tied rows the same rank without skipping, so Ava is 3rd.
The top student in each major
Add PARTITION BY and the numbering restarts in each partition. To keep only the top rows, rank them in a WITH query, then filter in the outer query:

props.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, major, gpa,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY major ORDER BY gpa DESC) AS major_rank
  FROM students
  WHERE gpa IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT major, name, gpa
FROM ranked
WHERE major_rank = 1
ORDER BY major, name;

content.text: keeps both. Pick the function that matches what you want for ties:
with a tiebreaker returns exactly one student per major. For the top three in each major, keep the rows where
is also a common way to keep exactly one row per group, such as each student's most recent enrollment: partition by student, order newest first, and keep row 1.
PostgreSQL has a few more ranking functions.
splits the ordered rows into four groups as close to equal in size as possible, which gives you quartiles, though it can put tied rows in different groups.
gives each row's relative rank as a number from 0 to 1. The

In PostgreSQL, NULL sorts as if it were larger than every other value, so ORDER BY gpa DESC puts students with no GPA first and ranks them 1st. Filter them out with WHERE gpa IS NOT NULL, or write ORDER BY gpa DESC NULLS LAST.

options.text: It depends on the students' names

props.question: Four students have GPAs of 3.9, 3.8, 3.8 and 3.5. Ranked from highest GPA to lowest, what does RANK give the student with 3.5?

content.text: Adding ORDER BY inside OVER changes what an aggregate sees. Without it,
adds up the whole partition. With it,
adds up the rows from the start of the partition through the current row, which gives you a running total.
Running totals usually follow time, so the window has to be ordered by something that sorts in time order. Suppose
holds the year and month each term starts, like
for spring 2026. This query adds up each student's credits per semester, then keeps a running total:

props.code:
WITH term_credits AS (
  SELECT e.student_id, e.semester, SUM(c.credits) AS credits
  FROM enrollments e
  JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
  GROUP BY e.student_id, e.semester
)
SELECT s.name, t.semester, t.credits,
       SUM(t.credits) OVER (PARTITION BY t.student_id ORDER BY t.semester) AS credits_so_far
FROM term_credits t
JOIN students s ON s.id = t.student_id
ORDER BY s.name, t.semester;

content.text: Here are Maya's rows from the result:
PARTITION BY restarts the total for each student, and ORDER BY semester decides which rows count as "so far".

Text sorts alphabetically, so names like Fall 2025 and Spring 2025 would put fall first, even though spring comes first in the year. Order a window by a date or another value that sorts in time order.
Looking back and ahead with LAG and LEAD
from the previous row in the window's order, and
returns it from the next row. On a partition's first row there's nothing to look back at, so
returns NULL. Both also take an offset and a default, so
returns 0 on the first row instead of NULL.
When several functions share a window, you can name it once in a
clause. This query compares each semester's load with the one before and after it:

props.code:
WITH term_credits AS (
  SELECT e.student_id, e.semester, SUM(c.credits) AS credits
  FROM enrollments e
  JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
  GROUP BY e.student_id, e.semester
)
SELECT s.name, t.semester, t.credits,
       LAG(t.credits) OVER w AS last_term,
       LEAD(t.credits) OVER w AS next_term,
       t.credits - LAG(t.credits) OVER w AS change
FROM term_credits t
JOIN students s ON s.id = t.student_id
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY t.student_id ORDER BY t.semester)
ORDER BY s.name, t.semester;

content.text: Here are Maya's rows, without the name column:
Look at fall 2025. Maya was on co-op in spring 2025 and took no courses, so she has no row for that semester.
compared fall 2025 with fall 2024, because it looks at the previous row, not the previous semester on the calendar.

With ORDER BY, a running total also includes any rows that tie with the current row. If a student had several rows per semester, each would show the total through the end of that semester. To add one row at a time, write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW after ORDER BY, and add a tiebreaker column so the order is predictable.

droplets.name: Study Strategies That Actually Work
droplets.description: Swap rereading and cramming for study habits that help you remember the material on exam day.
droplets.overview: Rereading and cramming feel productive, but they don't hold up well on exam day. This droplet covers the study habits that learning research supports, and how to use them in your CS courses.
droplets.funFact: Rubber duck debugging takes its name from a story in The Pragmatic Programmer, a 1999 book by Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, in which a programmer carries around a rubber duck and explains code to it.
learningObjectives: Use retrieval practice instead of rereading
Space out study sessions and mix problem types
Prepare for CS exams by tracing and writing code by hand
Walk into an exam practiced and rested

content.text: Rereading your notes and highlighting feel productive. The material starts to look familiar, so it feels learned. But recognizing something on a page isn't the same as recalling it on an exam, with nothing in front of you but the question.
Retrieval practice means pulling information out of your memory, for example by answering questions with your notes closed.

Studies of student learning consistently find that retrieval practice leads to better long-term memory than spending the same time rereading. Each time you pull an idea out of memory, it gets easier to recall the next time.
After a lecture, close your notes and write down everything you remember. Then open them and fill in what you missed.
Turn your notes into questions. Answering "What's the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?" does more for you than rereading the slide with the answer.
Use flashcards, and say or write each answer before you flip the card.
Try practice problems before you look at the worked example.
Testing yourself only helps if you find out what you got wrong. Check each answer against your notes, the textbook or a solution, and start your next session with the questions you missed.

Recalling is harder than rereading, and you'll get things wrong at first. That's normal. The effort of pulling an answer out of memory is part of what makes it stick, and every miss shows you exactly what to study next. Researchers call this kind of productive struggle a desirable difficulty.
Feeling familiar with your notes isn't the same as knowing them. Close them and test yourself to find out.

options.text: Rereading the chapter the night before the exam
Highlighting the key terms in your notes
Writing down everything you remember with your notes closed
Copying your notes into a neater notebook

props.question: Which of these is retrieval practice?

content.text: How you schedule your studying matters, not just how many hours you put in. Two changes to your schedule make the same hours count for more: spreading your sessions out and mixing problem types.
Cramming packs your studying into one long session right before an exam. It can get you through the next morning, but much of it fades soon after, just when the final needs it.

means studying the same material in several shorter sessions over days or weeks. Studies consistently find that spaced practice leads to longer-lasting memory than the same amount of time in one sitting.
A simple schedule for each lecture:
Quiz yourself on it the next day.
Quiz yourself again a few days later.
Revisit it a week or two after that, mixed in with newer material.
Flashcard apps that use spaced repetition do this scheduling for you, and show you the cards you miss more often.
, doing ten problems of one type before moving to the next, or

, mixing types in one session. Blocking feels smoother, because you know which method to use before you read the problem. An exam won't tell you which method to use, and interleaving makes you practice that choice. Studies of math and problem-solving practice often find that students who interleave do better on later tests, even though practice feels harder.
Here's what a week of spaced, mixed practice might look like in CS 3200:
After the joins lecture, write two join queries
Write three join queries from memory and check them
Solve a mixed set of join, GROUP BY and subquery problems
Quiz yourself on last week before starting the new topic
Spaced, mixed practice feels slower than cramming one topic at a time. That feeling doesn't mean you're learning less.

props.question: Spreading your study time over several days usually leads to better long-term memory than spending the same amount of time in one session.

content.text: Many CS exams ask you to read and write code with no computer to run it. Practice under the same conditions.
Before you run a snippet, predict exactly what it prints. Track every variable in a table as it changes:
stops before 5, so the loop ends after
is 4 and the code prints 6. If you predicted something else, you've found exactly what to review.

If your exam is on paper, practice on paper. Write complete functions by hand, with no autocomplete and no running. Then type your code in exactly as written and run it. Every error you find, from a missing colon to a loop that runs one time too many, is something to practice before the exam.

Explain a topic out loud to a friend, a study group or even a rubber duck. The moment you say "and then it just works", you've found a gap to fill. In a study group, take turns: each person teaches one topic, and the others ask questions.
If your instructor shares practice or past exams, take at least one under exam conditions: timed, closed notes and no phone. Use the rest to practice topic by topic.

Research on sleep and memory consistently finds that sleep helps you hold on to what you studied, and that losing sleep hurts attention and problem solving. An all-nighter trades a night of sleep for a few hours of tired review.
Don't spend the night before an exam learning new material. Review what you know with a short self-quiz, then go to bed.

props.question: Why is tracing code by hand good preparation for a CS exam?
props.correctAnswer: It makes you predict exactly what the code does step by step, the way exam questions do, so a wrong prediction shows you what you don't understand yet.

droplets.name: Preparing for Technical Interviews
droplets.description: Know what each round tests, solve problems out loud, and practice in a way that carries over to the real thing.
droplets.overview: Technical interviews test how you solve problems and explain your thinking, not just whether you reach the answer. This droplet covers what each round looks like, a step-by-step way to work through a coding problem out loud, and how to practice so it shows on interview day.
droplets.funFact: The word algorithm comes from Algoritmi, the Latin form of the name of al-Khwarizmi, a ninth-century mathematician who worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad.
learningObjectives: Describe the common rounds of a technical interview
Work through a coding problem out loud, from clarifying questions to tests
Improve a brute force solution with a dictionary
Practice with mock interviews, timed problems and patterns

content.text: Technical interviews vary by company, but most follow a similar path. If you know the rounds ahead of time, you can prepare for each one instead of guessing.
You solve timed coding problems alone on a website, usually graded by automated tests
Practice timed problems in the language you'll use
A short call about your background, interests and availability
Have a short summary ready of who you are and what you're looking for
One or two problems in a shared editor while you explain your thinking
Questions about how you've handled teamwork, conflict and mistakes
Prepare specific stories from projects, jobs and clubs
Several interviews in a row, often mixing coding and behavioral questions
Review your notes from earlier rounds and get a good night's sleep

Not every company uses every round. Some combine rounds or give a take-home project instead of a live problem, and a few ask you to design a larger system, though that's less common for co-op and intern roles.

When a company invites you to interview, ask the recruiter what each round covers, which languages you can use, and whether you'll run your code. It's a normal question, and the answers tell you what to practice.
The final answer is only part of a coding interview. Interviewers usually watch for:
Whether you understand the problem before you start writing code.
How clearly you explain your thinking as you go.
Whether your code works and is easy to read.
Whether you test it and catch your own bugs.
How you respond to hints. Using a hint well counts in your favor.
Interviewers are judging how you think and communicate, not just whether your final code is right.

Even technical interviews often include questions like "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate." Answer with one specific story: the situation, what you did, and how it turned out. Have a few ready from group projects, jobs and clubs.

options.text: Only whether your final code passes every test
How you understand the problem, explain your thinking and test your code
How quickly you can type a solution
Whether you've seen the problem before

props.question: What are interviewers usually evaluating in a coding interview?

content.text: Most coding problems can be worked through with the same six steps. Saying each step out loud shows the interviewer how you think, and it keeps you from rushing into code.
Restate the problem and ask about the inputs, the output and edge cases.
Work through a small example by hand, plus an edge case or two.
Describe the simplest correct solution and how fast it runs.
Look for repeated work you can remove.
Write the solution, explaining as you go.
Walk through your examples line by line, then the edge cases.
The interviewer says: given a list of integers and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target.
Can I use the same element twice? No. Is there always an answer? Not always, so return
if there isn't one. Can numbers repeat or be negative? Yes.
and a target of 9, the answer is indices 0 and 1, because 2 + 7 is 9. For
and a target of 6, it's 0 and 1, which checks that you never pair a number with itself.
Check every pair. It's correct, but it takes O(n²) time, because each number gets compared with every number after it.
For each number, the partner you need is

. Instead of searching the rest of the list for it, store each number you've seen in a dictionary that maps it to its index. Check for the partner before you add the current number, so a number can't pair with itself. Dictionary lookups take constant time on average, so one pass is enough: O(n) time, using O(n) extra space.
Explain each line as you write it:
Run your examples, then the edge cases:

props.code:
assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == (0, 1)
assert two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6) == (1, 2)
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == (0, 1)
assert two_sum([1, 2, 3], 100) is None
assert two_sum([], 5) is None
print("All tests passed")

content.text: Don't start coding until you and the interviewer agree on what the function takes and returns. Changing that halfway through costs more time than asking.

props.question: Why does the dictionary solution check for the partner before adding the current number?
props.correctAnswer: So a number can't be paired with itself. When you check first, the dictionary only holds earlier numbers, so any match is at a different index.

content.text: Solving problems silently at your desk isn't the same as interviewing. Practice the way you'll be tested: out loud, on a clock, and with someone watching.

Pair up with a friend and take turns. One of you picks a problem and plays the interviewer, and the other solves it out loud. Afterwards, the interviewer gives honest feedback. Was the approach clear? Did you test your code? Did you go quiet when you got stuck?
Coding clubs sometimes run mock interviews, and your co-op advisor may know of other options.

Set a timer for about as long as a real interview round, and take one problem all the way through: clarify, brute force, improve, code and test. When time's up, stop. If you didn't finish, study a solution, then come back a few days later and solve it again from scratch.
Reading a solution and nodding along isn't practice. Close it and write the code yourself.

You probably won't get a problem you've already practiced, but you will see familiar patterns. After each problem, name the pattern it used, so the next problem with the same clue is easier to recognize.
You need to find a matching pair or count things
A sorted list, or a string you can read from both ends
Check whether a word is a palindrome
The longest or shortest stretch of a list or string that meets a condition
Sorted data and a value to find
Find a student ID in a sorted roster
The fewest steps between two points in a grid or unweighted graph
Shortest path out of a maze
Visiting every node in a tree or every path in a graph
Maximum depth of a binary tree
Keep a log of the problems you miss, with the pattern and what tripped you up. Revisit them a few days later.
Send a short thank-you email to your recruiter or interviewer within a day.
Write down the questions you were asked and how you answered while you still remember them.
If you don't get an offer, ask the recruiter whether they can share feedback. Not every company does, but it's fine to ask.

props.question: Once you understand a solution you've read, you can count that problem as practiced.

droplets.name: Time Management for Busy Semesters
droplets.description: See where your hours go, plan each week, and keep your focus when every course wants your time.
droplets.overview: A busy semester has more work than free time, so a plan built on a guess falls apart fast. This droplet shows you how to find where your time goes, plan a realistic week, and protect the hours you set aside for focused work.
droplets.funFact: The Pomodoro Technique is named after the tomato-shaped kitchen timer that its creator, Francesco Cirillo, used as a university student, since pomodoro is Italian for tomato.
learningObjectives: Track a week to see where your time actually goes
Plan each week with a weekly review and time blocks
Break big assignments into steps with their own dates
Protect your focus with single-tasking and timed work sessions

content.text: Most plans fall apart because they're built on a guess about how much free time you have. Before you plan, find out where your hours actually go.
Pick a normal week, not exam week or a holiday. A few times a day, write down what you did since your last check, in rough 30-minute chunks. A notes app, a spreadsheet or your calendar all work.
Be honest. Twenty minutes of scrolling between classes counts, and so does the walk to the library. You're collecting information, not grading yourself.
A fixed commitment is anything that happens at a set time you can't easily move, like a lecture, a lab or a work shift.
Add your fixed commitments to your calendar as repeating events: classes, labs, work shifts, club meetings, commuting, meals and sleep. Then add up the hours. Here's one student's week:
A week has 168 hours, so this student has 68 left for homework, studying, errands, exercise, friends and rest. That's the real budget you're planning with.
Once you have a week of notes, look for three things:
When do you focus most easily? Save hard work, like problem sets, for those hours.
Short gaps, phone checks and tasks that took twice as long as expected add up fast.
A 50-minute gap between classes is enough to finish a reading or review your notes.

options.text: To prove to yourself how busy you are
To plan around the time you actually have
To fill every free hour with work
To find out which classes you can skip

props.question: What is the main reason to track an ordinary week before you make a plan?

content.text: A plan turns "I should work on the project" into a specific task at a specific time. Two habits do most of the work: a weekly review and time blocking.
Pick a fixed time each week, like Sunday evening, and spend half an hour looking ahead:
Collect every deadline, exam and meeting for the next two weeks from your syllabi and course sites.
Choose the few tasks that matter most this week.
Look back at last week. What didn't get done, and why?
Time blocking means putting tasks on your calendar like appointments. Be specific: "CS 3200 homework 4, questions 1 to 3" is a block you can start right away, and "study" isn't.
Put your hardest work in your best-focus hours.
Leave empty buffer time. People routinely underestimate how long their own tasks will take, a pattern psychologists call the planning fallacy.
When you miss a block, move it to a new time instead of deleting it.
Breaking big assignments into dated steps
A project due in three weeks feels like it can wait, until suddenly it can't. Break it into steps and give each step its own date. Here's a plan for a group database project due on Friday of week 3:
Read the spec and list questions for the TA
Agree on the schema with your team
Write and test the SQL queries
The last step lands a day before the deadline, which leaves room for something to go wrong.
If a step is too big to finish in one or two sittings, break it down again.

props.question: Your group's project is due in three weeks. How would you plan it so the work doesn't pile up at the end?
props.correctAnswer: Break it into steps, like designing the schema, writing the queries and drafting the report, give each step its own date, and block time for each one with a buffer before the deadline.

content.text: A plan only works if the time you block actually goes to the task. Three habits protect it: doing one thing at a time, keeping your phone away, and working in focused sessions.

Each time you switch tasks, it takes a while to get back into the first one. Research on task switching consistently finds that jumping back and forth makes work slower and more error-prone than finishing one thing at a time.
Close the tabs and apps you don't need for the current task.
Keep a "later" list. When something unrelated pops into your head, write it down and get back to work.
Put your phone out of reach

If your phone is on the desk, you'll check it. Put it in your bag or another room, and turn on Do Not Disturb or a focus mode while you work. If your laptop is the problem, log out of distracting sites or use a site blocker during work blocks.
The Pomodoro Technique gives your work a simple rhythm:
Set a timer for 25 minutes and work only on that task.
When the timer rings, take a short break of about 5 minutes.
After four sessions, take a longer break.
The exact lengths matter less than the rhythm of focused work and real breaks. If 50 minutes of work and a 10-minute break suit you better, use that.
A break that turns into an hour on your phone isn't a break. Stand up, stretch, refill your water or take a short walk instead.
Every new commitment takes time from something already on your calendar. Before you agree to an extra club role or a side project, check your week. Saying no can be short and polite:
"I can't take that on this semester, but thanks for thinking of me."
"I can help with the design, but I don't have time to lead it."
"Let me check my week and get back to you tomorrow."

droplets.name: Accessibility Basics for the Web
droplets.description: Build web pages that work for people using screen readers, keyboards or screen magnifiers.
droplets.overview: An accessible website works for everyone, including people who use screen readers, keyboards or screen magnifiers. This droplet covers who you're building for, the HTML habits that do most of the work, and quick ways to check your own pages.
droplets.funFact: Developers often shorten accessibility to a11y, because there are 11 letters between its first letter, a, and its last letter, y.
learningObjectives: Describe how people with different disabilities use the web
Choose semantic HTML elements instead of generic ones with click handlers
Write labels for form fields and alt text for images
Check a page with a keyboard test, a contrast checker and browser audits

content.text: Web accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use your site. Some disabilities are permanent and some are temporary, like a broken wrist. Situations can limit people too, like glare on a phone screen. Accessible design works better in all of these cases, and usually for everyone else too.
Many people who are blind or have low vision use a screen reader. Common ones include VoiceOver on Apple devices, NVDA and JAWS on Windows, and TalkBack on Android.

People who can't use a mouse, for example because of a motor disability, move through a page with Tab and Shift+Tab and operate controls with Enter, Space and the arrow keys. Others use devices that work like a keyboard, such as switches.
Many zoom in or use a screen magnifier, and strong contrast between text and its background helps them read.
Some can't tell certain colors apart, such as red and green, so color can't be the only way a page shows information.
People who are deaf or hard of hearing.
They need captions for videos and transcripts for audio.
People with cognitive or learning disabilities.
Clear language, consistent navigation and forms that explain their errors help them, and everyone else as well.
A screen reader is software that reads a page aloud or sends it to a braille display. It relies on your HTML to know what each part of the page is.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, or WCAG, are the most widely used standard for web accessibility. They're published by the W3C, an international organization that develops web standards, and they're built on four principles:
People can perceive the content in at least one way
Every button works from the keyboard
Content and controls are clear and predictable
Form errors explain how to fix them
Content works with browsers and assistive technology
Standard HTML elements are used correctly
Each guideline has testable success criteria at three levels: A, AA and AAA. Level AA is the usual target for websites and apps. The W3C's
publishes WCAG along with plain-language introductions and tutorials.
Accessible design helps more people than you'd expect. Captions help in a noisy dining hall, and strong contrast helps on a phone in bright sun.

props.question: Give an example of someone without a permanent disability who benefits from an accessible website, and explain how.
props.correctAnswer: A student watching a lecture video in a noisy room benefits from captions, and someone with a broken arm benefits from a site that works fully with a keyboard.

Placeholder text isn't a label. It disappears as soon as someone starts typing, and it's often too faint to read.

content.text: You don't need special software to find the most common problems. Three quick checks catch a lot of them.
Put your mouse aside and use the page with only the keyboard:
Press Tab repeatedly, starting from the top of the page. At every step, you should be able to see which element has focus.
Check that focus moves in a sensible order that matches the layout.
Make sure you can reach every link, button and form field, and use each one with Enter or Space.
Open each menu or dialog, then make sure you can close it and move on without getting stuck.
If Tab skips over links on a Mac, turn on keyboard navigation in System Settings, and in Safari's own settings if you test in Safari.
Never remove the focus outline with outline: none unless you replace it with another clear style. Without it, keyboard users can't tell where they are on the page.

Text needs enough contrast with its background for people with low vision to read it, and for everyone reading on a dim screen or in sunlight. Contrast is measured as a ratio, from 1:1 for two identical colors up to 21:1 for black on white. WCAG level AA sets these minimums:
Large text, at least 18 point or 14 point bold
In CSS terms, 18 point is 24px and 14 point is about 18.7px. For example, the gray
on white has a ratio of about 4.5:1, just enough for normal text, while the lighter

You don't need to calculate ratios yourself. In Chrome's DevTools, inspect some text and click its color in the Styles pane to see its contrast ratio. Firefox's Accessibility Inspector checks contrast too.
Contrast isn't the only rule about color. Don't use color alone to carry meaning: a form field that turns red when there's an error also needs an error message in words.

Browsers have built-in audit tools. In Chrome, open DevTools, select the Lighthouse panel, choose the Accessibility category and run the report. It flags problems like missing alt text, missing labels and low contrast. Firefox's Accessibility Inspector can check a page for similar issues.
Automated tools find only some problems. They can't tell whether your alt text makes sense or whether the focus order is logical, so always do the keyboard test too.
